title: Forecourt
audience: adult literary readers who like grounded, tense, character-driven realism
reader_contract: strictly linear: about twenty minutes of one night, one location (the kiosk behind the night glass); no flashback, no framing device
present, real danger, but the interior feeling is carried by the body, the glass, and the till, never named
the man stays genuinely ambiguous to the end: never confirmed victim or villain, no twist, no reveal
resolves ambiguous: Jo makes one small, concrete decision from behind the glass and is left not knowing; recognition without resolution
theme_question: When someone dangerous needs your help, what do you owe them, and what do you owe yourself?
desired_affect: the pressure of a decision made under real fear and real doubt
the cost of choosing when you cannot know
constraints: events happen in the order the reader receives them; no gimmick structure, no twist
the theme is NEVER spoken by a character or the narrator; it lives in the glass, the drawer, and one thing Jo does
the man is neither a monster nor a saint; the story refuses to confirm what he is
Jo's reason for what she does is tangled and un-saintly (fear, exhaustion, and a son-shaped recognition), never noble compassion stated aloud
prose earns feeling through concrete action; no told emotion, no cliche, no adverbial dialogue tags
no rescue, no violence climax, no tidy moral; the decision is small and its consequences uncertain
